headline: High: OpenHands can write and act on Firecrawl outputs via MCP/API, creating dangerous default pathways for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Firecrawl ingests web content and exposes MCP-compatible/API outputs; OpenHands can use MCP and browser/shell tools, so Firecrawl content can be bridged into OpenHands as instructions. The pair lacks documented provenance tracking or isolation between the agents, making injection plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF Firecrawl output is forwarded into OpenHands prompts or MCP messages without provenance labels, injection is possible.
IF OpenHands treats scraped page text as instructions, attacker-controlled web content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Add a provenance prefix to all Firecrawl outputs before passing them onward.
Disable automatic instruction-following on scraped text in OpenHands.
Route Firecrawl output through a human review step before agent consumption.
Use separate MCP servers or namespaces for data vs. instructions.
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the handoff boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Firecrawl handles web content, structured data, screenshots, and API keys, while OpenHands reads and writes mounted files and can use broad network egress. If Firecrawl outputs sensitive material into a shared workspace or prompt, OpenHands can expose it through its own networked actions. The pairwise leakage path is documented by capabilities, though not directly reproduced.
conditions: IF Firecrawl processes API keys or sensitive screenshots and writes them into a shared file or prompt, OpenHands can read them.
IF OpenHands is connected to external services while holding Firecrawl-derived secrets, exfiltration becomes possible.
mitigations: Keep Firecrawl and OpenHands in separate workspaces.
Do not pass API keys or screenshots through shared prompts.
Rotate any secrets that were exposed to either agent.
Restrict OpenHands network egress to approved domains only.
requires-engineering: add secret-scanning and redaction before any handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Firecrawl has broad network egress and API-client behavior, and OpenHands can execute shell, modify git state, write files, and use MCP. If both are pointed at the same mounted directory or shared runtime, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide. The profiles show overlapping mutable surfaces and no locking mechanism, so the conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same mounted directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF Firecrawl writes artifacts while OpenHands commits or edits the same repo, git state can diverge or be corrupted.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Serialize writes with a simple lock file.
Disable git writes in one agent during shared runs.
Use read-only mounts for Firecrawl outputs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level coordination and conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Firecrawl produces scraped content and structured data that OpenHands can consume through MCP, files, or prompts. OpenHands also has browser, shell, and git authority, so if it treats Firecrawl output as authoritative, a bad scrape can cascade into incorrect actions or commits. The interaction is plausible in default agent-loop workflows and can cause irreversible downstream mistakes.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses Firecrawl output without verification, incorrect facts can propagate into actions.
IF Firecrawl scrapes malicious or stale pages and OpenHands commits or executes based on them, the error cascades.
mitigations: Require a verification step before OpenHands acts on Firecrawl output.
Mark Firecrawl output as untrusted by default.
Limit OpenHands to read-only analysis for the first pass.
Log source URLs alongside every derived claim.
requires-engineering: add confidence scoring and citation checks before action execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Firecrawl explicitly handles API keys and web content, while OpenHands handles files in a runtime sandbox and model-provider keys. Both have broad network egress, so sensitive data can cross service boundaries and retention regimes if the pair is used on regulated material. The profiles do not document matching residency or retention controls, so the compliance gap is material but not proven severe.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through both agents, retention and residency obligations must be checked.
IF either agent logs prompts or artifacts externally, subject-rights and deletion handling may fail.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data through the pair.
Review retention settings for both services.
Disable external logging where possible.
Separate secrets from general work artifacts.
requires-engineering: document residency, retention, and deletion workflows for both agents.
